name: Pacahuara
confidence_why: Tallman 2018, the only first-hand account of Pacahuara prosody, states outright that its prosodic system is not understood and that the pitch patterns of its words differ from Chácobo in every case, and no other work on the language (Fleck 2013, Oliveira 2014, SAPhon, the ELAR deposit) says anything about its stress, so the record can only be left undetermined.
catalog_citation: Tallman, Adam J. R. 2018. A Grammar of Chácobo, a southern Pano language of the northern Bolivian Amazon. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin. hdl:2152/74212 (open access).
catalog_locator: §1.11 'Some tentative notes on Pacahuara or Tapanahua', pp. 33-38; glottal-stop bullet p. 36, deciding paragraph p. 38.
catalog_quote: Some salient phonological and phonetic differences between Chácobo and Pacahuara are summarized below ... Glottal stop in first or second syllable: In Chácobo vowel-vowel sequences glottal stops do not occur in coda position. In Pacahuara a glottal stop occurs in the coda position of the first syllable of a lexical item as in (1.1). It is unclear whether this is related to metrical structure or prominence. In Pacahuara the glottal stop does not occur when the first syllable has the highest pitch (or high tone?) as shown in (1.2). ... The surface pitch patterns of Pacahuara lexical items elicited in isolation tend to be distinct from Chácobo in all cases. Nearly all of phonological differences stated above make reference to the supposed prosodic categories (prominent syllable, tone, stress) of Pacahuara. But the prosodic system of Pacahuara is not understood and so the statements are at best tentative starting points for analysis. ... Pacahuara should be studied in its own right not as derivative or dialectal variant of Chácobo.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule: the sole first-hand source states that Pacahuara's prosodic system (stress/tone/prominence) is not yet understood; isolated words show pitch patterns different from Chácobo, and a first-syllable coda glottal stop alternates with first-syllable highest pitch, possibly prominence-related.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author flags possible Chácobo interference in all Pacahuara data (speakers bilingual, heavy contact).
new_statements.domain_note: Observations are on lexical items elicited in isolation (citation forms) with surface pitch transcribed; no word- vs phrase-level analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Tallman 2018 §1.11 describes the speech of the single remaining Tapanahua (Pacahuara) family living among the Chácobo at Puerto Tujuré (3 speakers in 2018), which he treats as a language distinct from Chácobo (chac1251); Fleck 2013 and SAPhon treat Pakawara as a dialect of Chácobo. The Chácobo stress rule (stem-initial by default, second syllable if H-toned) is NOT asserted for Pacahuara by Tallman, who says Pacahuara surface pitch patterns differ from Chácobo 'in all cases'. East & East's 1969-70 SIL 'Pacaguara' microfiches document an earlier generation of (presumably) the same group.
